course_description: Predicting the Past asks not what we can recover from the archaeological record, but how we come to know the past at all. The course connects theory directly to method and practice: how a theoretical position shapes what questions get asked, what evidence is sought, and what interpretations become possible. Students will examine the major theoretical approaches that have shaped archaeological reasoning, from culture-history and processualism to post-processual, Indigenous or materialist perspectives, and engage with current disciplinary debates around positionality and the co-production of knowledge with communities. Built around critical reading, active seminars, and the development of research frameworks, the course teaches students to assess the theoretical and methodological underpinnings of research designs and account for their own position in producing knowledge.

course_aims:
1. To familiarise students with the range and variety of contemporary archaeological theory.

2. To allow students to gain an understanding of the history of archaeological thought.

3. To allow students to confidently cross the divide between the present archaeological record and past human behaviour.

4. To provide students with a solid grounding in archaeological theory in preparation for Honours in archaeology or entry to the archaeological workplace.

learning_outcomes.description: Describe the major theoretical frameworks used in archaeology and their philosophical foundations
Analyse how theoretical and methodological choices shape the questions archaeologists ask, the evidence they pursue, and the interpretations they can defensibly make
Assess arguments and interpretive positions, recognising the influence of reflexivity, positionality, and differing cultural values on the production of archaeological knowledge
Research, synthesise and communicate evidence and analysis effectively

learning_activities.topic: Theory is your friend Theory isn't a lineage of dead ancestors to memorise in order, it's a living network of approaches, authors and assumptions, connected underground long before they surface that can really help you 'do archaeology'. This week introduces the mycelial metaphor, names the threads that we'll follow all semester, and invites you to engage reflexively with theory in your own practice. Learning outcomes: L02, L03

Setting the substrate: the foundations of archaeological theory We begin digging into the foundations of archaeological theory, tracing the three early and influential trends that still shape the discipline: culture history, processualism and post-processualism. Learning outcomes: L01, L02

Breaking dualities: theory in the new millennium Moving past the processual/post-processual split, we unpack how the threads from Week 1 help us see the origins of archaeological theory differently. This week we'll begin a weekly 'mushroom framework' seminar section that will look at the practical applications of theory to research design, in preparation for the conceptual framework assessments. Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04

Practice theory; agency and structure This week we'll start to look beyond the processual/post-processual divide and unpack practice theory, agency and social structure. Student presentations (processualism; post-processualism; or middle range theory) will occur at the start of the seminar. At the end of the seminar, we will also continue the 'mushroom framework' work that will look at the practical applications of theory to research design, in preparation for the conceptual framework assessments. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Identity, gender and personhood This week we explore personhood, gender and identity as things made rather than given, drawing on feminist and queer theory to ask how archaeology has both obscured and recovered them. Student presentations (praxis; practice theory; agency) will occur at the start of the seminar. At the end of the seminar, we will also continue the framework seminar section that will look at the practical applications of theory to research design, in preparation for the conceptual framework assessments. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

The secret lives of things Can personhood extend beyond people? We explore object agency and the biography of things, and where these ideas overlap with behavioural archaeology. Student presentations (queer theory; feminism; gender) will occur at the start of the seminar. At the end of the seminar, we will also continue the framework seminar section in preparation for the conceptual framework assessments. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Experiencing the past We turn to the experiential past, exploring landscape phenomenology and materiality; how bodily, sensory engagement with place and things has been used (and contested) as a route into past lives. This week we'll also contrast this with other approaches to environmental interactions studied through cultural ecology and systems theory. Student presentations (Object biography; behavioral archaeology; object agency) will occur at the start of the seminar. At the end of the seminar, we will also continue the framework seminar section in preparation for the conceptual framework assessments. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

In class exam on Conceptual Framework Design For this exam, you'll be given an archaeological problem and, using the theories from class, will need to design a conceptual framework to address it, then reflect on and justify the choices you made. Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04

Networks of things We follow the mycelial metaphor to its theoretical home, tracing a line through contextual archaeology, Act or-Network theory and new materialisms, and asking what archaeology gains when humans stop being the only actors in the story. This is the week the metaphor turns reflexive: the course's own model is up for critique. Student presentations (phenomenology; systems theory; cultural ecology; or optimal foraging theory) will occur at the start of the seminar. At the end of the seminar, we will also continue the framework seminar section in preparation for the conceptual framework assessments. Learning outcomes: L01, L03
Mid-semester break Not dead time! The network rests underground before it fruits...
Study break (public holiday) Not dead time! The network rests underground before it fruits...

More-than-human: people, plants and animals We frame the week through evolutionary theory, then open it into multispecies archaeology: archaeology's role in understanding the long, entangled relationships between people, plants and animals. Student presentations (new materialisms; contextual archaeology; actor network theory) will occur at the start of the seminar. At the end of the seminar, we will also continue the framework seminar section in preparation for the conceptual framework assessments. Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04

Breaking from colonised things We bring postcolonial theory, Indigenous knowledges and the ontological turn to the foreground, asking who gets to narrate the past, and what it means to take colonised things and other ways of knowing seriously. Student presentations (more-than-human; multispecies; evolutionary theory) will occur at the start of the seminar. At the end of the seminar, we will also continue the framework seminar section in preparation for the conceptual framework assessments. Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04

New relations: a conclusion We close by stepping back to map the mycelium that was there all along. Not "where we ended up on the tree" but the living network in all its messy forms, ready for your contributions. Learning outcomes: L02, L03
